lessons.title: Labour markets and wages
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Economics — Labour markets; market failure; government intervention; national income (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain the demand for and supply of labour.
Use diagrams to analyse the effect of a minimum wage.
Describe the role of trade unions and causes of wage differentials.
reviewNotes: Prices and quantities are invented teaching figures in FCFA, not real market data.
The legal minimum wage in Cameroon (SMIG) is mentioned only in general; its current level and rules must be checked before use.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Demand for labour
blocks.md: Firms hire labour as a **derived demand**: the demand for workers depends on the demand for the product. A profit-maximising firm hires workers up to the point where the wage equals the **marginal revenue product (MRP)** of labour: MRP = marginal physical product × marginal revenue (price in competition). Because of diminishing returns, the MRP curve (the demand curve for labour) slopes downward.

blocks.title: Supply of labour and the wage
blocks.md: The **supply of labour** to an occupation is upward-sloping: higher wages attract more workers. It shifts with **qualifications required, working conditions, migration, population, and wages in other jobs**. In a competitive labour market the **equilibrium wage** is where demand equals supply. **Wage differentials** reflect skills, training costs, risk, responsibility, and **market power** (including trade unions and monopsony employers).

blocks.caption: Labour market: a minimum wage above equilibrium causes unemployment.
blocks.alt: Downward demand-for-labour line and upward supply line crossing at E, with a dashed horizontal minimum-wage line above the intersection.

blocks.title: Minimum wages: both sides of the evaluation
blocks.md: A **minimum wage** above the equilibrium creates a surplus of labour (unemployment) in a competitive market model, but raises the wage of those who keep jobs and may improve motivation and reduce poverty. The size of the unemployment effect depends on the **elasticity** of demand for labour and on whether employers have monopsony power. Do not just state 'it causes unemployment': show it on a diagram and evaluate. Minimum-wage rules and enforcement in Cameroon should be checked from official texts.

blocks.title: Trade unions and wage setting
blocks.md: A **trade union** bargains collectively; it can raise wages above equilibrium by restricting supply (closed shop, licences) or raising productivity/threatening strikes. Possible costs: unemployment among excluded workers, higher costs, strikes. The **informal sector** (market traders, taxi drivers, small farmers) sets earnings largely by competition with little regulation or union cover.

blocks.title: Worked example — MRP
blocks.statement: A worker produces 5 extra kg of groundnut paste per hour (MPP) and each kg sells for 400 FCFA. Calculate MRP and say whether to hire at a wage of 1800 FCFA per hour.
steps: MRP = MPP × price = 5 × 400 = 2000 FCFA per hour.
The wage is 1800, which is less than MRP of 2000.
So hiring adds 200 FCFA of profit per hour: hire.

blocks.title: Worked example — minimum wage
blocks.statement: Labour demand: W = 30 − 2L; supply: W = 6 + 2L (W in hundreds of FCFA per hour, L in hundreds of workers). Find the equilibrium; then the effect of a minimum wage of 24.
blocks.answer: Equilibrium: W 18, L 6; with minimum wage 24, unemployment = 6 hundred workers

lessons.title: Market failure
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Economics — Labour markets; market failure; government intervention; national income (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define market failure and list its main causes.
Analyse negative externalities with a diagram and measure the welfare loss.
Explain public goods, merit and demerit goods and information failure.
reviewNotes: Prices and quantities are invented teaching figures in FCFA, not real market data.
Local examples (river pollution) are generic; do not name real companies.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Market failure
blocks.md: **Market failure** occurs when the free market leads to an **inefficient** allocation of resources (or an unfair one). Main causes: **externalities**, **public goods**, **merit and demerit goods**, **information failure**, **monopoly power** and **immobility of factors**, plus an **inequitable** distribution of income. At the market output, **marginal social cost (MSC) differs from marginal social benefit (MSB)**, causing a **welfare loss**.

blocks.title: Externalities
blocks.md: An **externality** is a cost or benefit to a third party. **Negative production externality** (e.g. a factory dumping waste in a river): MSC > MPC (marginal private cost), so the market output exceeds the social optimum and price is too low. **Positive externality** (e.g. vaccination, education): MSB > MPB, so too little is produced. The **welfare loss** is the triangle between MSC and MSB over the excess output.

blocks.caption: A negative externality: market output (10) exceeds the social optimum (8).
blocks.alt: Demand line and two upward lines for private and social costs, with points marked at the market and socially optimal outputs.

blocks.title: Public goods versus merit goods
blocks.md: A **public good** is **non-excludable** (cannot stop non-payers using it) and **non-rival** (one person's use does not reduce another's); the **free-rider problem** means private firms do not provide it (defence, street lighting). A **merit good** (education, health care) **can** be sold privately but is **under-consumed** because people undervalue the benefits or lack information; a **demerit good** (tobacco) is over-consumed. Do not say that any good provided by the state is a public good.

blocks.title: Other failures
blocks.md: **Information failure**: consumers lack knowledge (e.g. counterfeit medicines). **Monopoly power**: higher price and lower output. **Factor immobility**: structural unemployment. **Inequality**: markets reward ability to pay, not need. Governments may respond with taxes, subsidies, regulation, provision, information campaigns or tradable permits, but may suffer **government failure** (poor information, cost, unintended consequences).

blocks.title: Worked example — externality
blocks.statement: Demand (MSB): P = 22 − Q; MPC: P = 2 + Q; MSC: P = 6 + Q. Find the market output and the socially optimal output.
steps: Market: 22 − Q = 2 + Q gives Q = 10 and P = 12.
Social optimum: 22 − Q = 6 + Q gives Q = 8 and P = 14.

blocks.title: Worked example — welfare loss
blocks.statement: Using the same data, calculate the welfare loss at the market output.
steps: At Q = 10, MSC = 16 and MSB = 12: the gap is 4.
The gap falls to 0 at Q = 8: a triangle.

lessons.title: Government intervention in markets
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Economics — Labour markets; market failure; government intervention; national income (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Analyse the effects of indirect taxes, subsidies and price controls using diagrams and calculations.
reviewNotes: Prices and quantities are invented teaching figures in FCFA, not real market data.
Taxes in Cameroon (VAT, customs duties) are mentioned only generally here; rates and rules must be checked.
Government failure is introduced only briefly.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Taxes and subsidies
blocks.md: An **indirect tax** (e.g. VAT or excise) raises costs, so supply shifts **upward/left** by the amount of the tax. The price rises by **less than the tax** (unless demand is perfectly inelastic) and quantity falls. **Tax incidence** is the share of the tax borne by consumers (rise in price) and by producers (fall in net price). A **subsidy** lowers costs, shifting supply right: price falls and quantity rises; it costs the government money.

blocks.title: Price controls
blocks.md: A **maximum price (ceiling)** below the equilibrium price causes **excess demand** (shortage), queues and black markets (e.g. rent control, price caps on essentials). A **minimum price (floor)** above equilibrium causes **excess supply** (e.g. guaranteed prices for farmers, minimum wages); the government may have to buy the surplus. **Regulation** (standards, licences, competition law) and direct **provision** and **public ownership** are other tools.

blocks.caption: A tax of 3 shifts supply from S to S + tax: the price rises from 8 to 10 and quantity falls from 6 to 5.
blocks.alt: Demand line and two upward supply lines, the second above the first, with points marked for the original and new equilibrium.

blocks.title: Who pays the tax?
blocks.md: Do not assume the whole tax is passed on to consumers. The more **inelastic** demand is relative to supply, the more the burden falls on consumers; the more elastic demand, the more falls on producers. To measure incidence use the **price rise** for consumers and the **fall in net price** (after the tax) for producers. The tax revenue is tax per unit × new quantity, not the old quantity.

blocks.title: Evaluating government action
blocks.md: Intervention may improve efficiency or equity but there may be **government failure**: poor information, administration costs, unintended consequences (black markets, smuggling), political pressure, and delays. Evaluate by considering the **size** of the market failure, **elasticities**, **costs**, **time lags** and **who gains and loses**.

blocks.title: Worked example — tax incidence
blocks.statement: D: P = 20 − 2Q; S: P = 2 + Q (P in hundreds of FCFA). A tax of 3 per unit is imposed. Find the new equilibrium, who bears the tax and the revenue.
steps: New supply P = 5 + Q: 20 − 2Q = 5 + Q gives Q = 5 and P = 10 (before: Q = 6, P = 8).
Consumers pay 10 − 8 = 2 more per unit: 10 in total; producers keep 10 − 3 = 7, i.e. 1 less per unit: 5 in total.

blocks.title: Worked example — maximum price
blocks.statement: With the same market (before the tax), a maximum price of 6 is imposed. Find the shortage.

lessons.title: National income and the circular flow
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Economics — Labour markets; market failure; government intervention; national income (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the circular flow of income and the three methods of measuring national income.
Calculate GDP, GNI, real GDP, per capita figures and growth rates.
Evaluate GDP as a measure of living standards.
reviewNotes: Prices and quantities are invented teaching figures in FCFA, not real market data. The imaginary economy is not Cameroon.
Illustrative scale used; do not interpret as Cameroon's GDP.
The split of topics between Lower and Upper Sixth is an editorial choice to be checked against the GCE Board syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: National income measures
blocks.md: **GDP** (gross domestic product) is the total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a year. Three equivalent methods: **output** (value added in all sectors), **income** (wages, rent, interest, profit) and **expenditure**: **GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)**. **GNI** = GDP + net income from abroad. **Net** means after deducting capital consumption (depreciation). **Per capita** = GDP ÷ population.

blocks.title: Circular flow
blocks.md: Households supply factors to firms and receive income; they spend on goods. Saving (S), taxes (T) and imports (M) are **leakages**; investment (I), government spending (G) and exports (X) are **injections**. National income is in equilibrium when **leakages = injections**. **Nominal** GDP uses current prices; **real** GDP removes inflation: real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price index × 100.

blocks.caption: The circular flow of income between households and firms, with injections and leakages.
blocks.alt: Two boxes, households and firms, joined by arrows for spending and for factor incomes, with text lines for injections and leakages.

blocks.title: What GDP leaves out
blocks.md: GDP counts only **final** goods (to avoid double counting) and excludes unpaid work, most of the **informal economy** and the value of leisure, and does not subtract environmental damage. A high GDP per capita does not mean that income is evenly shared. Do not compare nominal GDP over time; compare **real** GDP. Transfer payments (pensions, grants) and second-hand sales are not included in GDP.

blocks.title: Living standards
blocks.md: Better indicators combine GDP per capita with the **Human Development Index** (income, education, life expectancy), poverty and inequality measures, and environmental data. International comparisons use **purchasing power parity** exchange rates. Growth in real GDP per capita is a rough guide to improvements in material well-being.

blocks.title: Worked example — GDP and GNI
blocks.statement: An imaginary economy has C = 12 000, I = 3000, G = 2500, X = 2400, M = 2900 (billion FCFA) and net income from abroad of −400. Calculate GDP and GNI.
steps: GNI = GDP + net income from abroad = 17000 − 400 = 16600 billion FCFA.

blocks.title: Worked example — real GDP and growth
blocks.statement: Using the nominal GDP of 17 000 with a price index of 125 (base year 100), find real GDP. If real GDP next year is 14 076, find the growth rate. Population is 20 million; find GDP per capita.
blocks.answer: Real GDP 13 600; growth 3.5 %; per capita 850 000 FCFA
